To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the decision maker's endogenous beliefs are not consistent with the standard expected utility model; and that (2) the mean-variance-skewed preferences imply that the cross-section of asset expected returns is related to the skewness of the asset returns, and that the cross-section is not linear in asset betas.

(1) endogenous beliefs and disappointment aversion can lead to a preference for safe assets and to under-diversification; (2) investors with mean-varaince-skewness preferences can improve their investment opportunity set by holding additional assets, and (3) the cross-section of returns can be explained by the first three moments.
• Endogenous beliefs can be used to explain the underreaction to news and overreaction to past returns.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how preferences and expectations interact in a decision making context.
the question of whether investors can benefit from additional information and how this information is priced in financial markets.
the implications of preferences which go beyond mean-variance preferences for portfolio choice and asset returns.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the standard expected utility approach is a very good approximation of the real world decision making process.

this thesis contributes to the literature in the following three ways: (1) it shows the implications of endogenous belief formation for portfolio choice and asset prices and (2) it derives the implications of mean-variance-skewed preferences for the investment opportunity set and asset pricing, and (3) it provides a new approach for testing the implications of skewness preferences in the cross-section of stock returns.
the results of our empirical tests support the notion that the mean-variance-skewed utility model can explain asset pricing anomalies and cross-sectional asset pricing phenomena.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an endogenous belief model which is a generalization of the standard expected-utility model.
we show that preferences which go beyond expected utility and mean variance preferences are relevant for explaining asset prices.
investors' beliefs are endogenous to their preferences and their beliefs affect their preferences.
The main takeaway from our work is that

endogenous beliefs and preferences for the skewness of portfolio returns have important implications for the portfolio choice and asset allocation decisions of individual investors, as well as for the equilibrium pricing of risky assets.
investors with endogenous beliefs can exhibit a preference for skewness and that the presence of additional risky assets can be beneficial to these investors.
the standard model of expected utility is too restrictive.
